vignette:
Patient Name: Mr. A.
Age: 58
Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician (Retired, now a consultant)
Therapist's Notes (Session 4):

Mr. A. enters my office with a measured, deliberate gait. He sits, but does not relax. His hands rest on his knees, palms flat, as if bracing for a sudden jolt. He is a compact man, fifty-eight, with a graying beard and eyes that scan the room's exits before they settle on me. He speaks in a low, precise voice, the kind used to describe the wiring of an IED. But today, he is not describing a bomb. He is describing his son.

The story begins in 2017. Mr. A. was forty-three, a senior technician with a decade of service in the Indian Army's bomb disposal unit. He had dismantled hundreds of devices. He describes the work as a kind of prayer: slow, reverent, absolute. "You do not think of your wife. You do not think of your son. You think only of the wire. The wire is God." He says this without irony.

Then his son, Arjun, then eight, was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Mr. A. was on a six-month deployment in Kashmir. He received the news via a satellite phone call from his wife, Priya. He remembers the exact temperature of the air that day-forty-two degrees Celsius-and the way the dust on his boots looked like dried blood.

He did not come home. He could not. The unit was short-staffed, and the next technician was a trainee. He told himself that Arjun was in good hands, that the doctors were the real experts. He stayed. He dismantled bombs. He called home every night, listening to Priya's voice, thin and frayed, as she described the chemo, the hair loss, the fevers. He offered tactical advice. "Stay calm. Follow the protocol." He was a good soldier.

The trauma, he tells me, did not happen in a single moment. It was a slow, cumulative detonation. The moment he did come home-six months later-Arjun was in remission, but the boy did not recognize him. He looked at his father the way one looks at a stranger who has arrived too late to a fire.

That was seven years ago. Arjun is now a healthy fifteen-year-old. Mr. A. retired from active disposal three years ago, taking a desk job as a consultant. He should be grateful. He is not.

He describes his current life as a state of constant, low-grade vigilance. He cannot sit with his back to a door. He checks the locks on his house three times before bed. He has not slept through the night since 2018. The hypervigilance, he says, is not about bombs. It is about the phone. He keeps his mobile phone on his nightstand, volume max, ringer on. He waits for the call. The call that says the cancer is back. The call that says Arjun has relapsed. He knows this is irrational. He knows the boy is healthy. But his body does not know.

He has intrusive images, but they are not of war. They are of a hospital room he never saw. He imagines the IV drip, the sterile white sheets, his son's small hand reaching for a father who is not there. He sees this image at stoplights, during meetings, while his wife is speaking to him. He feels a pressure in his chest, a tightness in his throat, and a sudden, overwhelming urge to run. He does not run. He sits. He waits.

His marriage is strained. Priya tells him he is "gone," that he came back from Kashmir but never came home. He does not argue. He knows she is right. He feels a profound disconnection from her, from his son, from the life he saved. He feels like a wire that has been cut. He is still. He is safe. But nothing is connected.

He has no nightmares. Instead, he has a recurring state of semi-wakefulness. He lies in bed, eyes open, listening to the hum of the refrigerator, the creak of the house. He is waiting for the explosion. He knows it will not come. But his body, trained for a decade to read threat, cannot unlearn the script. The threat is gone. The wiring remains.

He scores a 39 on the PCL-5. He does not ask for the number. He asks only, "Is there a way to stop the waiting?"
